questions.stem:
(a) State four signs that show that a sow is about to farrow. [4 marks]
(b) Describe the management of a pregnant sow from mating to farrowing. [8 marks]
(c) Describe four management practices carried out on piglets during the first three weeks after birth. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) Any four, 1 mark each: swelling and reddening of the vulva; enlargement of the udder/milk can be squeezed from teats; restlessness; nest-building behaviour (gathering bedding); loss of appetite; frequent urination
8 marks: (b) Any four described, 2 marks each: confirm pregnancy (no return to heat after 21 days); feed a balanced gestation ration and avoid over-fattening; increase feed (steaming up) in the last weeks; provide clean water; deworm and treat for external parasites before farrowing; move to a clean, disinfected farrowing pen with guard rails about one week before farrowing; provide clean dry bedding; avoid rough handling and fighting; wash the sow before moving
8 marks: (c) Any four described, 2 marks each: ensure piglets suckle colostrum soon after birth; clip needle teeth to prevent injury to the sow's teats and littermates; iron injection (at 3 days) to prevent anaemia; navel cord cut and dressed with iodine; ear notching/tagging for identification; tail docking; castration of male piglets not for breeding; provide heat (brooding lamp/creep area); start creep feeding from about 2 weeks
questions.explanation: A sow near farrowing shows a swollen vulva, milk in the teats, restlessness and nest-building. During pregnancy she is fed a balanced ration with steaming up near term, dewormed and moved to a clean farrowing pen with guard rails a week before farrowing. Piglets receive colostrum, have needle teeth clipped, get iron injections, navel care, identification, warmth and creep feed.

questions.stem:
(a) Name the parts of the oviduct of a hen and state what is added to the egg in each part. [10 marks]
(b) State four conditions necessary for successful artificial incubation of chicken eggs. [4 marks]
(c) Describe how a day-old chick brooder should be prepared and managed during the first two weeks. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Infundibulum: receives the ovum/site of fertilisation (chalazae begin)
2 marks: (a) Magnum: most of the albumen (egg white) is added
2 marks: (a) Isthmus: shell membranes are added
2 marks: (a) Uterus (shell gland): water, salts and the shell (calcium carbonate) and pigment are added
2 marks: (a) Vagina: egg is held and laid; protective cuticle (bloom) added
4 marks: (b) Any four, 1 mark each: temperature of about 37.5 oC; relative humidity about 55-60% (higher at hatching); adequate ventilation; turning of eggs several times daily (until day 18); clean, fertile eggs of good size and shape; candling to remove infertile eggs
6 marks: (c) Any three described, 2 marks each: clean and disinfect the house and equipment before arrival; spread clean dry litter (wood shavings) and cover with paper; provide heat source (lamp/charcoal) and pre-heat to about 32-35 oC, reducing gradually; use a chick guard to keep chicks near heat; provide clean water with glucose/vitamins and chick mash in shallow feeders; observe chick behaviour to adjust heat; vaccinate as scheduled (e.g. Newcastle, Gumboro)
questions.explanation: The ovum is caught and fertilised in the infundibulum; albumen is added in the magnum, shell membranes in the isthmus, shell in the uterus, and the egg is laid via the vagina. Incubation needs about 37.5 oC, correct humidity, ventilation and regular turning. A brooder is cleaned, littered, pre-heated with a chick guard, supplied with water and chick mash, and heat adjusted by watching the chicks.

questions.topic: Processing techniques for different farm animal products
questions.stem:
(a) Describe the processing of fresh cow milk into yoghurt. [8 marks]
(b) State four methods of preserving meat. [4 marks]
(c) Explain four ways of improving the marketing of animal products in Nigeria. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Filter fresh milk and heat (pasteurise) to about 85-90 oC to kill microorganisms
2 marks: (a) Cool to about 40-45 oC
2 marks: (a) Inoculate with starter culture (Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus) and incubate at about 42-45 oC for 4-6 hours until it sets
2 marks: (a) Cool, add flavour/sugar/fruit if desired, package in clean containers and refrigerate
4 marks: (b) Any four, 1 mark each: refrigeration/freezing; smoking; drying (e.g. kilishi); salting/curing; canning; boiling and frying
8 marks: (c) Any four explained, 2 marks each: provision of cold storage and processing facilities; good rural roads and transport; formation of co-operatives for bargaining power; grading and standardisation of products; market information services; hygienic abattoirs and markets; credit to marketers; advertising and attractive packaging; reduction of middlemen
questions.explanation: For yoghurt, milk is filtered, heated, cooled to about 43 oC, inoculated with a Lactobacillus/Streptococcus starter, incubated until set, then flavoured, packaged and chilled. Meat is preserved by chilling, freezing, smoking, drying, salting or canning. Marketing improves with cold chains, roads, co-operatives, grading, market information, hygienic facilities and credit.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between selection and breeding as methods of animal improvement. [4 marks]
(b) Explain the following breeding systems, giving one advantage of each: (i) inbreeding; (ii) outbreeding (outcrossing); (iii) crossbreeding; (iv) upgrading (grading up). [12 marks]
(c) A local hen is mated with an exotic cockerel, and the female offspring are mated back to exotic cockerels for two more generations. What percentage of exotic genes is expected in the third generation of offspring? [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Selection: choosing animals with desirable traits as parents of the next generation and culling undesirable ones
2 marks: (a) Breeding: the controlled mating of selected animals to produce offspring with desired combinations of traits
3 marks: (b)(i) Inbreeding: mating of closely related animals (e.g. sire to daughter); advantage: fixes desirable traits/produces uniform animals
3 marks: (b)(ii) Outbreeding: mating of unrelated animals of the same breed; advantage: reduces inbreeding depression/increases vigour
3 marks: (b)(iii) Crossbreeding: mating of animals of different breeds; advantage: hybrid vigour (heterosis) / combines good traits of both breeds
3 marks: (b)(iv) Upgrading: repeated mating of local females and their female offspring to purebred (exotic) males over generations; advantage: gradually improves local stock cheaply while retaining adaptation
2 marks: (c) F1 = 50% exotic; F2 = (50 + 100)/2 = 75%
2 marks: (c) F3 = (75 + 100)/2 = 87.5% exotic genes
questions.explanation: Selection chooses superior parents; breeding controls their mating. Inbreeding fixes traits, outbreeding restores vigour, crossbreeding gives heterosis and upgrading gradually raises local stock towards an exotic breed. In upgrading, exotic genes rise from 50% to 75% to 87.5% by the third generation.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between endoparasites and ectoparasites, giving two examples of each. [6 marks]
(b) Describe the life cycle of a one-host tick, and state three harmful effects of ticks on cattle. [8 marks]
(c) State three methods of controlling internal parasites and three methods of controlling external parasites of farm animals. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a) Endoparasites live inside the host body (gut, liver, blood)
2 marks: (a) Examples, any two: liver fluke; tapeworm; roundworm (Ascaris); coccidia; trypanosomes
1 mark: (a) Ectoparasites live on the body surface of the host
2 marks: (a) Examples, any two: ticks; lice; mites; fleas; tsetse fly; biting flies
5 marks: (b) Engorged female drops off host and lays thousands of eggs on the ground; eggs hatch into six-legged larvae which climb vegetation and attach to a host; larvae feed, moult to eight-legged nymphs on the same host; nymphs feed and moult to adults on the same host; adults mate and the engorged female drops off (all stages on one host)
3 marks: (b) Any three, 1 mark each: suck blood causing anaemia; transmit diseases (e.g. babesiosis/redwater, heartwater, anaplasmosis); damage hides; cause irritation and wounds that attract flies; reduce weight gain and milk yield; tick paralysis
3 marks: (c) Internal, any three: regular deworming/drenching; rotational grazing; clean water and feed; control of intermediate hosts (snails); proper disposal of faeces; good hygiene
3 marks: (c) External, any three: dipping or spraying with acaricides; hand-picking ticks; pasture burning/rotation; clean housing; dusting with insecticide; pour-on treatments
questions.explanation: Endoparasites (liver fluke, tapeworm) live inside the host; ectoparasites (ticks, lice) on its surface. A one-host tick completes larva, nymph and adult stages on one host; the engorged female drops to lay eggs. Ticks cause anaemia, transmit redwater and heartwater, and damage hides. Deworming, rotational grazing and snail control manage endoparasites; dipping, spraying and hand-picking manage ectoparasites.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe the intensive, semi-intensive and extensive systems of livestock management. [9 marks]
(b) State three advantages and two disadvantages of the intensive system. [5 marks]
(c) Describe the deep litter system of keeping laying hens, stating three items of equipment needed in the house. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) Intensive: animals confined in houses/pens throughout; all feed, water and care provided by the farmer; high capital and labour input
3 marks: (a) Semi-intensive: animals housed for part of the time (e.g. at night) and allowed to graze/roam in fenced areas for part; supplementary feeding
3 marks: (a) Extensive: animals roam freely to find their own feed and water with little or no housing or care
3 marks: (b) Advantages, any three: better disease control; efficient feed use and higher productivity; protection from thieves and predators; easy record keeping; less land needed
2 marks: (b) Disadvantages, any two: high capital cost; high labour and feed costs; rapid spread of disease if outbreak; vices such as cannibalism; needs skilled management
3 marks: (c) Birds kept on the floor of a well-ventilated house covered with litter (wood shavings, rice husks, groundnut shells) 5-10 cm deep; litter turned regularly and replaced when wet/caked; stocking about 3-4 birds per square metre
3 marks: (c) Any three equipment, 1 mark each: feeders; drinkers; laying nests; perches; lamps/lighting; litter fork/rake
questions.explanation: Intensive systems confine animals with full care; semi-intensive systems combine housing and grazing; extensive systems let animals roam with little care. Intensive systems give good control and productivity but cost more and spread disease quickly. Deep litter houses layers on 5-10 cm of absorbent litter, turned regularly, with feeders, drinkers, nests and perches.
